steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper reporting an observational study of how cannabis intoxication affects programming. Motivate it with what prior surveys found and the policy debate, describe the study design briefly, list our contributions, and mention the policy implications and our replication package.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Cannabis use among developers and the lack of firm understanding
2. Prior studies of programmers' cannabis use
3. Negative views in broader contexts; anti-cannabis policies
4. What an effective study would need
5. Our study and contributions
6. Implications and replication package

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- developers commonly use psychoactive substances while programming; at odds with company drug and hiring policies
- Cannabis sativa ("cannabis"): world's most common illicit substance; more than 192 million users in 2018; market of 20.5 billion USD
- claims, biases, folk wisdom about effects on programming disagree
- no firm understanding -> no informed policy decisions; can't balance risk and reward

2. Prior studies
- 2022 study: 800 programmers (450 full-time developers); 35% used cannabis while programming; 18% at least once per month
- motivations: enjoyment, more creative solutions, brainstorming, focus
- 2023 study: interviews, 25 professional programmers using psychoactive substances: positive on brainstorming; neutral on coding, testing; negative on debugging, design, documentation
- part of historical tradition of software; advocates tout focus and creativity benefits

3. Broader contexts
- views more negative
- impairs decision-making accuracy and consistency; losses under-estimated [quote: losses treated as constant and minor]
- impairs motor control, reaction times [quote: crash risk]
- these views inform general and software-specific regulation
- anti-cannabis hiring/retention policies prevalent in software companies; almost one-third of developers took a drug test for a programming job
- questions about efficacy of such policies; whether needed or beneficial in modern context

4. Requirements
- understanding impacts on aspects of software development -> evidence-based corporate policies, informed developer decisions
- indicative sample size; ecologically-valid conditions; quantitative and qualitative aspects of produced software
- ethical conduct, rapidly-changing legal landscape

5. Our study
- first rigorous observational study; n=74 participants; multiple American metropolitan areas; four states; pre-registered hypotheses
- two sessions on different days (sober / cannabis), randomly-assigned order; within- and between-subjects comparisons
- short targeted tasks + multiple LeetCode problems; Visual Studio; personal computers
- cannabis condition: usual amount used while programming (ecologically valid)
- contributions: (1) first rigorous study; (2) small-medium effect on correctness, 10% more failed test cases, p<0.05; (3) 11% more time on non-trivial functions, p=0.39; (4) more deleting/rewriting, longer pauses, p\leq 0.003, d\geq 0.35; (5) no difference in algorithmic or stylistic choices; (6) accurate recognition of own performance, r=0.59

6. Implications
- low impact vs individual differences + recognition of impairment -> caution on anti-cannabis policies (Section 7)
- first study of its kind; design (pre-registered, ecologically valid, broad pool) -> generalizable, useful for policies and individual decisions
- de-identified replication package: raw data, stimuli, analysis scripts, design documents

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Software developers often use psychoactive substances while they program, and this behavior is at odds with many company drug and hiring policies. Cannabis sativa (or “cannabis”) is the most common illicit substance in the world. More than 192 million people used it in 2018 and it represents a market of 20.5 billion USD. The claims, biases, and folk wisdom about what cannabis intoxication actually does to programming do not agree with each other. Because there is no firm understanding, individuals and companies cannot make informed policy decisions or balance risk and reward accurately.

A 2022 study of 800 programmers (450 of them full-time developers) found that 35% had used cannabis while programming, and 18% did so at least once a month. Their motivations included enjoyment, thinking of more creative programming solutions, better brainstorming, and better focus. A 2023 study interviewed 25 professional programmers who used psychoactive substances. They had positive views on how cannabis affects brainstorming, neutral views on coding and testing, and negative views on debugging, design, and documentation. Psychoactive substances including cannabis are seen as part of the historical tradition of software, and advocates claim focus and creativity benefits.

In broader contexts the views can be more negative. Cannabis intoxication can impair the accuracy and consistency of decision-making, so that losses are under-estimated (“treating each loss as a constant and minor negative outcome regardless of the size of the loss”). It can also impair motor control and reaction times. For example, “acute cannabis intoxication is associated with a statistically significant increase in motor vehicle crash risk”. These more negative views often inform regulation, both general and specific to software. Anti-cannabis hiring and retention policies are common in software companies (for example in some companies' own policies), and almost one-third of developers said they had taken a drug test for a programming job. But questions have been raised about whether such policies are effective and whether they are either needed or beneficial in a modern context.

What an effective study would need
- understanding impacts on aspects of software development -> evidence-based corporate policies, informed developer decisions
- indicative sample size; ecologically-valid conditions; quantitative and qualitative aspects of produced software
- ethical conduct, rapidly-changing legal landscape

Our study
- first rigorous observational study; n=74 participants; multiple American metropolitan areas; four states; pre-registered hypotheses
- two sessions on different days (sober / cannabis), randomly-assigned order; within- and between-subjects comparisons
- short targeted tasks + multiple LeetCode problems; Visual Studio; personal computers
- cannabis condition: usual amount used while programming (ecologically valid)
- contributions: (1) first rigorous study; (2) small-medium effect on correctness, 10% more failed test cases, p<0.05; (3) 11% more time on non-trivial functions, p=0.39; (4) more deleting/rewriting, longer pauses, p\leq 0.003, d\geq 0.35; (5) no difference in algorithmic or stylistic choices; (6) accurate recognition of own performance, r=0.59

Implications
- low impact vs individual differences + recognition of impairment -> caution on anti-cannabis policies (Section 7)
- first study of its kind; design -> generalizable, useful for policies and individual decisions
- de-identified replication package: raw data, stimuli, analysis scripts, design documents

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Software developers often use psychoactive substances while they program, and this behavior is at odds with many company drug and hiring policies. Cannabis sativa (or “cannabis”) is the most common illicit substance in the world. More than 192 million people used it in 2018 and it represents a market of 20.5 billion USD. The claims, biases, and folk wisdom about what cannabis intoxication actually does to programming do not agree with each other. Because there is no firm understanding, individuals and companies cannot make informed policy decisions or balance risk and reward accurately.

A 2022 study of 800 programmers (450 of them full-time developers) found that 35% had used cannabis while programming, and 18% did so at least once a month. Their motivations included enjoyment, thinking of more creative programming solutions, better brainstorming, and better focus. A 2023 study interviewed 25 professional programmers who used psychoactive substances. They had positive views on how cannabis affects brainstorming, neutral views on coding and testing, and negative views on debugging, design, and documentation. Psychoactive substances including cannabis are seen as part of the historical tradition of software, and advocates claim focus and creativity benefits.

In broader contexts the views can be more negative. Cannabis intoxication can impair the accuracy and consistency of decision-making, so that losses are under-estimated (“treating each loss as a constant and minor negative outcome regardless of the size of the loss”). It can also impair motor control and reaction times. For example, “acute cannabis intoxication is associated with a statistically significant increase in motor vehicle crash risk”. These more negative views often inform regulation, both general and specific to software. Anti-cannabis hiring and retention policies are common in software companies (for example in some companies' own policies), and almost one-third of developers said they had taken a drug test for a programming job. But questions have been raised about whether such policies are effective and whether they are either needed or beneficial in a modern context.

If we understood how cannabis intoxication impacts specific aspects of software development, this would help fill the knowledge gap, and it would allow corporate policies based on evidence and informed decisions by developers about when and if to use cannabis while programming. An effective understanding would need an indicative sample size, ecologically-valid conditions, and both quantitative and qualitative aspects of the software that is produced. Also, any study like this has to be conducted ethically, because the legal landscape around cannabis use is changing rapidly.

We conducted the first rigorous observational study of what cannabis intoxication does to programming. We assessed n=74 participants from multiple American metropolitan areas in four states, and we used pre-registered hypotheses to mitigate researcher bias. Every participant did two sessions on different days, one sober and one while using cannabis, in an order that was randomly assigned. With this design we can do both within-subject and between-subjects comparisons. In each session the participants did short targeted programming tasks and also multiple LeetCode problems, using a standard development environment (Visual Studio) on their own personal computers. In the cannabis condition we asked participants to use the amount they would normally use while programming. This is an ecologically-valid context, so we can learn actionable insights from it. Our contributions are:

- (1) The first rigorous observational study of programming both sober and while intoxicated with cannabis.

- (2) We find that ecologically-valid cannabis intoxication has a small to medium effect on program correctness: programs that cannabis-intoxicated programmers write have more bugs and fail 10% more test cases on average (p<0.05).

- (3) Cannabis-intoxicated programmers take more time than sober programmers to write non-trivial functions (11% more time on average, p=0.39).

- (4) Cannabis-intoxicated programmers have different typing patterns, for example they delete and rewrite code more often and they pause for longer without typing (p\leq 0.003, d\geq 0.35).

- (5) There are anecdotes about cannabis improving creativity, but we see no evidence that cannabis-intoxicated programmers make different algorithmic or stylistic programming choices.

- (6) Programmers who use cannabis recognize their programming performance accurately, even when they are intoxicated, r=0.59.

Cannabis has a low impact compared to individual differences, and developers can recognize when cannabis impairs them, which suggests caution when anti-cannabis policies are made (see Section 7).

As far as we know, this is the first study of how cannabis intoxication impacts programming. We think that parts of our design (pre-registered hypotheses, ecologically-valid settings, broad participant pool, etc.) make it generalizable and useful to inform policies and individual developer decisions about cannabis. We make our (de-identified) replication package available, with raw data, stimuli, analysis scripts, and design documents.
